transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc... I guess I'm here because I had a bit of an outburst. I completely blew up at one of the younger volunteers the other day. It was over a crooked tablecloth, if you can believe that. 

We were setting up for the luncheon, and they always use those cheap plastic covers now. You know the ones? They smell like chemicals and stick to your arms. Back in the day, we used real linen. My wife would spend all Saturday ironing them, making sure there wasn't a single wrinkle. You just don't see people putting in that kind of effort anymore, everything's just rush, rush, rush. And the tables they use now, they always have that one short leg so the whole thing wobbles every time someone sets down a coffee cup... 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. The kid had the tablecloth all lopsided, and I just lost my temper. Yelled right at him. I don't usually talk to people that way. I really don't. It's just not like me at all to do something like that.
Has this kind of outburst happened to you before?

No, no, I really haven't. Like I said, it's just not me. I've always been a pretty even-keeled guy, you know? Even back when I was working at the plant, and things would get real hectic on the floor... I was a foreman, see, and you had to keep a level head. If you started yelling, the guys wouldn't respect you. I remember one time, Jimmy—he was this young kid, couldn't have been more than nineteen—he dropped a whole pallet of spark plugs. Thousands of 'em, just rolling everywhere. Sounded like a waterfall of metal. You'd think I would've been furious, but I just sighed, got the broom, and helped him sweep 'em up. That broom had a splintery handle, too. Always meant to tape it up, but never got around to it. You know how those little chores just pile up? Like fixing the hinge on the screen door... I've been meaning to do that since Tuesday. But anyway, no, blowing up at people? That's not my style. I don't know what got into me with that tablecloth.
Has anything significant changed in your life recently?

Well, I suppose... I mean, this whole being on edge thing, it's been going on for about a week now. Ever since that robbery happened right outside the bank. I was just going to deposit my pension check, you know? They still mail the paper checks if you ask them to. I like having the paper in my hand. My daughter keeps telling me to set up the direct deposit on the computer, but I don't trust those machines. You hear all these stories about hackers stealing people's identities. Just last month, my neighbor, Mrs. Gable—lovely woman, makes a fantastic rhubarb pie—she got an email saying she owed the IRS ten thousand dollars. Can you imagine? She was practically in tears. Turned out it was a scam, of course. But you just can't be too careful these days. The world's going to hell in a handbasket, if you ask me. Used to be you could leave your front door unlocked, and the milkman would just bring the bottles right into the kitchen... oh, but yeah, it's been about a week since the bank thing.
Did the robbery outside the bank upset you more than you thought it would?

Well, I didn't think so at the time, but... I don't know. It's like I can't shake it. Out of nowhere, I'll just be sitting at my kitchen table—it's a nice oak table, you know, bought it at a Sears Roebuck back in '74. Solid wood, not like that particle board junk they sell at Ikea these days. My wife always kept a lace doily right in the center with a little bowl of hard candies. Peppermints, mostly. I still buy them, even though my dentist tells me I shouldn't. Dr. Henderson, he's a good guy, but he charges an arm and a leg for a simple cleaning. Anyway... I'll just be sitting there, having my morning coffee, and suddenly I hear that man's rough voice right in my head. Just barking orders. Or I'll see the donation envelope hitting the ground, clear as day, like I'm right back on that sidewalk. It's awful strange. I was just looking at the envelope, thinking about how they changed the color of them. Used to be a nice pale blue, now they're this bright, obnoxious yellow. Makes no sense to me. But yeah, it just pops into my head when I'm not even trying to think about it.
Do you feel like you're reliving the robbery when these memories pop into your head?

Well, exactly, yeah. Like I was just telling you, it's like I'm right back there. One minute I'm just sitting at my kitchen table minding my own business, and the next, out of nowhere, I hear that man's rough voice echoing in my head again, or I see that envelope hit the pavement. It feels so real, like it's happening all over again right in front of me. 

It's just like... well, you know how sometimes your senses can play tricks on you and take you right back? Like my wife's pot roast. Sometimes I swear I can smell it cooking in the oven. She used to make it every single Sunday. Always put a little splash of red wine in the gravy. I told her it was a waste of good wine at first, but it really gave it a kick. We used to get our wine from this little shop down on 4th street. The fella who ran it, Tony, he had this mustache that curled right up at the ends. Looked just like one of those old-timey cartoon characters. He closed up shop back in '98, I think. Or maybe '99. Shame, really. You just can't find good, personal service like that at the big supermarkets nowadays. You go into a Kroger and nobody even looks you in the eye. 

But, uh... what was I saying? Oh, right, the bank thing. Yeah, when those flashes happen with the voice and the envelope, it definitely feels like I'm reliving the whole awful mess.
Have you been avoiding places or activities that remind you of the robbery outside the bank?

Well, I suppose I have been, yes. I've been taking the long way around when I go for my morning walk, just so I don't have to pass by that bank. It adds about four blocks to my route, which isn't terrible, I guess. Gets the blood pumping. My doctor—Dr. Aris, not the dentist, the general practitioner—he's always telling me I need to keep moving. Says at my age, the joints rust up if you don't use them. He's a young fella, probably not even forty yet. Wears these bright, colorful socks with his fancy suits. Last time I was in, he had flamingos on his ankles. Flamingos! Can you believe it? In my day, a professional man wore black or navy socks. Period. Maybe brown if he was wearing a tweed suit, but that was pushing it. My father was a tailor, you know. Worked down in the garment district for forty-five years. He could spot a cheap suit from across the street. He always said, "A man is only as good as the cut of his trousers." 

But, uh, where was I? Oh, the bank. Yes, I avoid walking past it. And I haven't gone into the festival storage room at the community center, either. I usually help organize the fall festival—been doing it for twelve years now—but I just can't bring myself to go in that room. It just brings the whole thing too close, you know? Makes me feel all tight in the chest.
Have you been having any nightmares about the robbery?

Well, no, not really. I don't think I've had any bad dreams about it. Honestly, I don't remember my dreams much anymore anyway. Usually I just sleep right through the night, unless I have to get up to use the washroom. Which happens more often than I'd like to admit these days. My prostate isn't what it used to be. Dr. Aris gave me some pills for it, little orange things. They taste awful if you don't swallow them fast enough. Reminds me of this orange soda we used to get when I was a kid. Nehi, it was called. Oh, that stuff was sweet. We'd save up our pennies all week just to get a bottle on a hot summer afternoon. We'd sit on the porch steps—my childhood home had these big, wide wooden steps, painted a dark forest green. My mother repainted them every spring without fail. She was a stickler for keeping the house looking sharp. She'd be out there with her brush, wearing this big straw hat with a yellow ribbon. 

But anyway, no, I haven't been waking up in a sweat or anything like that. Just regular sleep, mostly.
Do you find yourself being more aware of your surroundings than usual, like you're constantly on the lookout for something?

Not really, no. I wouldn't say I'm constantly on the lookout or anything like that. I mean, I've always been a bit observant, just by nature. I like to sit by the front window in the afternoons with my tea and just watch the neighborhood go by. You see all sorts of things if you just sit still. Like Mrs. Gable from across the street. She's always out there fussing with her petunias. I swear, that woman waters them three times a day. It's a wonder the poor things haven't drowned yet. Her husband, Frank, he used to have the most beautiful lawn on the block before he passed. Cut it on a diagonal, just like a baseball outfield. He worked at the Chevy plant for thirty-something years before his back gave out. Good union man, Frank was. We used to go bowling down at the alley on 5th Street every Thursday night. Had a team called the Pin Pounders. We even got matching shirts one year, bright blue with our names stitched over the pocket in white thread. Mine shrank in the wash, though, my wife accidentally put it on hot... 

But, uh... I'm sorry, what was the question? Oh, being on the lookout. Right. No, I'm not really looking over my shoulder or feeling jumpy. Just keeping an eye on the street the same as I always have.
Do you find yourself jumping or startled more easily than you used to, even by small surprises?

Well, yes, I suppose I have been. Just the other day I was walking near the senior center. I go there for the Tuesday morning card games. Pinochle, usually, though sometimes they rope me into bridge. I'm not much for bridge, too much counting, but Arthur insists. Arthur used to be an accountant for the city, so he loves all that math stuff. He's got this little mustache he actually waxes at the ends, looks like something out of an old black-and-white movie. He buys the wax special from some catalog. 

Anyway, I was outside the center, and this car drove past and backfired. Goodness, I jumped so hard my chest actually hurt. My hands just kept shaking for a few minutes after, too. I couldn't even get my keys out of my pocket to unlock my own front door when I got home. You just don't hear cars backfire like that anymore, you know? With all the computers they put in engines these days, they run so quiet. My first car was a '54 Chevy, and that thing rattled so loud you couldn't hear yourself think. The muffler fell right off on Main Street once, just clattered right down onto the pavement in front of the diner. The waitress, Betty, she came out laughing... 

But, what were we talking about? Oh, right, being startled. Yes, that car backfiring really gave me a terrible fright. Shook me right up.
How long have you been feeling this way since the robbery outside the bank?

Well, it's been about a week now. Just a week since that awful business outside the bank. I usually go to that branch on Elm Street every Friday morning to get cash for the weekend. I like to have crisp bills, you know? The tellers there are always so nice about it. Especially Sarah, she's a lovely girl. She always asks about my grandson, Tommy. He's at college now, studying engineering of all things. I don't know where he gets the brains for it. His father, my son, he can barely fix a leaky faucet without calling a plumber. I remember when he tried to fix the sink in the downstairs bathroom... oh, it must have been 1985 or so. He ended up flooding the whole hallway. The carpet squished when you walked on it for a week. We had to rent one of those big wet-vacs from the hardware store. Old Mr. Henderson ran the place back then, always had a cigar stub hanging out of the corner of his mouth. He never actually lit it, just chewed on it... 

But yes, to answer your question, it's been about a week since the robbery. Just a week.
Are there any other activities or places you've been avoiding since the robbery happened outside the bank?

Well, I suppose I have been changing my routine a bit. I've been taking the long way around town just so I don't have to pass by that bank. It means I have to walk all the way down Maple Street now, which isn't so bad, really. The oak trees there are just lovely this time of year. My wife and I planted an oak when we first bought our house back in '72. Bought it as a little sapling from a nursery out in the county. The fellow who sold it to us, Jim, he had a glass eye. Always made me wonder how he lost the real one, but you know, it seemed rude to ask. He wore these thick wool sweaters even in the dead of summer. Said it kept the mosquitoes off, but I think he just liked the pockets. 

But... oh, what was I saying? Right, avoiding places. Yes, so I don't go near the bank. And I haven't gone into the festival storage room at the community hall, either. It just... it brings the whole thing too close, you know? I usually help sort the decorations for the autumn jubilee this time of year. We have these big orange and yellow banners we hang right across Main Street. Last year, the wind caught one and it got tangled right up in the traffic light. Took the fire department an hour to get it down with their ladder truck. Chief Miller was hollering at the young volunteers the whole time. He's got a voice like a foghorn, that man... 

But anyway, yes. I just can't bring myself to go in that storage room right now. Or go anywhere near the bank.
Have you noticed any difficulties in your daily life or relationships since the robbery happened outside the bank?

Well, yes, I suppose it has been making things difficult. I haven't been able to keep up with organizing the Día de los Muertos event the way I usually do. I'm usually the one who coordinates the marigold orders, you know. We get them from a wholesale place a few towns over. The fellow who runs it, Carlos, he's been doing it for thirty years. He used to drive this beat-up old green pickup truck, the kind with the wooden side panels. I always told him he should get it painted, but he said the rust gave it character. He's got a dog, too, a big golden retriever mix named Buster who just sleeps right in the middle of the greenhouse aisles. You have to step right over him, and he doesn't even open an eye... 

But, oh, right, the event. Yes, I just haven't been able to focus on it. And I've stopped going to my card nights, too. I just... I don't feel steady around people right now. I used to go every Thursday. We'd play rummy, mostly. Sometimes poker if Frank was feeling lucky. Frank always wears these loud Hawaiian shirts, even in December. He says it keeps his spirits up. He buys them from a catalog that sells nothing but tropical clothing and, for some reason, novelty bird feeders. He got one shaped like a pirate ship once, but the squirrels figured out how to get into the rigging and ate all the suet in one afternoon... 

Anyway, yes. No card nights, and I'm falling behind on the festival planning. It's just too much right now.
Have you been feeling guilty or ashamed about anything related to the robbery outside the bank?

Guilty? No, no, I don't think so. I mean, I didn't do anything wrong, did I? I was just standing there. Though, speaking of feeling guilty, my neighbor Mrs. Gable felt terribly guilty just the other day. She backed her car right over my prized petunias. Flattened the whole flowerbed by the mailbox. She drives this enormous beige Lincoln Town Car, you know the kind? They look like boats sailing down the street. My uncle Arthur used to drive a boat of a car like that, a '76 Cadillac Fleetwood. Oh, he loved that thing. Washed it every single Sunday morning with a special chamois cloth he ordered out of a catalog. He wouldn't let anyone else touch the paint, not even his own kids. His youngest boy, Bobby, once drew a little smiley face in the dust on the trunk, and Arthur chased him around the yard with the garden hose for a good ten minutes. Bobby ended up joining the Navy, actually, stationed out in San Diego. I always wondered if that hose incident had something to do with him liking the water... 

But, oh, what were you asking? About the robbery. Right. No, no guilt or shame or anything like that. Just... just trying to get by.
Are there any other activities or daily routines you've stopped doing because they remind you of the robbery?

Well, let me think... no, I don't think there's anything else I've stopped doing. I still go down to the bakery every morning for my coffee, even though it's a bit of a walk now with my new route. The girl who works the counter there, Sarah, she always saves me a blueberry muffin. She's a sweetheart, really. Just got engaged to a boy who works over at the hardware store. He's a nice enough fellow, but he's got this habit of chewing on toothpicks all day long. I asked him once if he was trying to quit smoking, but he said no, he just likes the taste of the wood. Reminds me of my grandfather, actually. He used to whittle these little wooden figures on the front porch. Bears, mostly, sometimes an owl if the wood had a good knot in it. He gave me one for my tenth birthday, a little bear standing on its hind legs. I kept it on my dresser for years until my mother accidentally knocked it off while dusting and chipped its ear. She tried to glue it back on, but she used that old hide glue that smells like wet dog, and it never quite looked the same...

But, um, what was the question? Oh, routines. Right. No, I think I've mentioned everything. Just avoiding the bank and the storage room, mostly.
Do you find yourself constantly looking over your shoulder or feeling like you're waiting for something bad to happen?

Well, no, not constantly, I don't think. I'm not waiting for anything bad to happen, really. Though my sister, Margaret, she's always waiting for the other shoe to drop. She reads those horoscopes in the Sunday paper like they're gospel. Last week it told her to beware of sudden financial changes, so she went and took all her money out of the credit union and hid it in a coffee can under the sink. It's a Folgers can, the big red plastic ones they make now. Not like the old tin ones. Remember those? My dad used to keep nails in them in the garage. He had dozens of them lined up on a shelf, all labeled with masking tape and a black marker. He had a very specific system for his nails—galvanized, finishing, roofing—and if you put one back in the wrong can, oh, you'd hear about it for a week. He built a whole shed out back just using scrap wood he found behind the old lumber yard. The yard shut down back in... oh, it must have been '85. They built a strip mall there instead, got one of those frozen yogurt places where you pull the levers yourself. I tried the tart flavor once, but it just tasted like sour milk...

But, right, looking over my shoulder. No, I wouldn't say I do that. I just go about my day, you know?
Have you felt detached from yourself or the world around you since the robbery happened outside the bank?

Detached? Hmm. No, I wouldn't say that. I feel like myself, mostly. I mean, the world's still the world, isn't it? Though, speaking of the world, my buddy Frank just bought one of those big globe bars for his living room. You know, the ones that look like an antique map of the earth, and then you open the equator and there's bottles of scotch inside? He got it at an estate sale over in Oak Creek. The house belonged to some retired judge who collected clocks. Hundreds of them, Frank said. Grandfather clocks, cuckoo clocks, little mantel clocks that chimed every fifteen minutes. I'd go crazy with all that ticking. I used to have a wristwatch that ticked so loud I had to leave it in the kitchen drawer at night just to get some sleep. It was a Timex, one of those with the expandable metal bands that always pinches the hair on your arm. My wife bought it for me for our silver anniversary. We went to a nice steakhouse that night, the one downtown that burned down a few years ago. They had the best baked potatoes, the size of a football, loaded with real bacon bits, not that artificial stuff that comes in a jar...

But, uh, what were we talking about? Detached. Right. No, no, I don't feel detached or anything like that. Just regular old me.
Do you find yourself being overly alert or watchful, even when there's no apparent reason to be?

Watchful? Well, no, I wouldn't say that. I'm not really on edge or anything. Although, speaking of watchful, my neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she's practically the neighborhood watch all by herself. Sits at her front window all day with a pair of binoculars. Those heavy black ones, you know? They look like they belong on a Navy battleship. My uncle Arthur was in the Navy. Served on a destroyer in the Pacific back in the day. He used to send us postcards from all over—Hawaii, the Philippines. He brought back this beautiful silk robe for my mother once, embroidered with these big gold dragons. She wouldn't wear it, though, said it was too fancy for just making breakfast, so she hung it up in the cedar closet upstairs. That closet always smelled so strong, gave me a headache if I stayed in there too long looking for my winter coat. We had these heavy wool coats back then, not like the thin, shiny puffy things people wear now. You'd put one of those wool ones on and feel like you were carrying a sack of potatoes on your shoulders. And if it got wet in the snow? Forget about it, took three days to dry out over the radiator... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, being overly alert. Right. No, no, I just mind my own business, really. I don't feel the need to be on the lookout.
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy doing?

Lost interest? No, I wouldn't say that. I still like my usual routine. I go down to the senior center on Tuesdays for pinochle, same as always. Though, speaking of pinochle, my friend Gary just bought one of those automatic card shufflers. You know, the plastic ones where you split the deck and press a button and it zips them together? Makes a terrible racket. He got it from one of those mail-order catalogs. He gets dozens of them in the mail, the ones selling gadgets you don't really need, like heated steering wheel covers or flashlights that double as radios. I bought a radio flashlight once, back in '99 when everyone was worried about that Y2K bug. We stocked up on canned beans and bottled water. My wife, God rest her soul, she bought so much Spam we were eating it for three years after nothing happened. Spam sandwiches, Spam and eggs, baked Spam with cloves stuck in it like a little ham. It's actually not half bad if you fry it up crispy in a cast-iron skillet. You gotta season the skillet right, though, with a little oil and heat, otherwise everything just sticks to the bottom and it's a nightmare to clean. Cast iron lasts forever if you treat it right. My mother had a pan that must have weighed ten pounds...

But, uh, what were you asking me? Losing interest. Right. No, no, I still enjoy my cards and everything else. Just keeping busy, you know?
Are there any other places, people, or activities that you've been avoiding since the robbery happened outside the bank?

Avoiding things? Well, I suppose... I mean, I have been taking the long way around when I drive to the grocery store so I don't have to pass that bank. And I haven't gone into the festival storage room at the community center, either. It just brings the whole thing too close, you know? Being in there, with all those boxes. Though, speaking of boxes, my daughter Sarah just sent me this enormous care package in the mail. It was packed to the brim with those little foam peanuts. I hate those things, they get everywhere. You open the box and suddenly it looks like it snowed in your living room. They stick to your clothes, the carpet, the cat... Oh, the neighbor's cat, Barnaby, he got into a box of them once and came out looking like a marshmallow. Barnaby's a Maine Coon, huge thing, must weigh twenty pounds. He likes to sleep on top of my car in the summer, leaves these big dusty paw prints all over the windshield. I used to wash my car every Sunday, out in the driveway with a bucket of soapy water and a big yellow sponge. You don't see people doing that much anymore, do you? Everyone just goes to those automatic washes where the big floppy brushes slap against the windows. I went through one of those once and it ripped the antenna right off my old Buick. That was a great car, a '78 LeSabre, rode like a boat on a calm lake. Had these plush velour seats that were so comfortable you could fall asleep at a red light...

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, avoiding things. Yeah, just the bank and the storage room. I just stay away from those spots.

I was just looking at the envelope, thinking about how they changed the color of them. Used to be a nice pale blue, now they're this bright, obnoxious yellow. Makes no sense to me. But yeah, it just pops into my head when I'm not even trying to think about it.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient is experiencing flashbacks
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're reliving the robbery when these memories pop into your head?

target_item.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: Out of nowhere I hear that man's rough voice in my head or see the donation envelope hitting the ground, even when I'm just sitting at my kitchen table.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient feels like they are reliving the robbery when the memories pop up, which directly relates to intrusive symptoms and flashbacks (recurrent, involuntary memories of the traumatic event).

patient.answer:
Well, exactly, yeah. Like I was just telling you, it's like I'm right back there. One minute I'm just sitting at my kitchen table minding my own business, and the next, out of nowhere, I hear that man's rough voice echoing in my head again, or I see that envelope hit the pavement. It feels so real, like it's happening all over again right in front of me. 

It's just like... well, you know how sometimes your senses can play tricks on you and take you right back? Like my wife's pot roast. Sometimes I swear I can smell it cooking in the oven. She used to make it every single Sunday. Always put a little splash of red wine in the gravy. I told her it was a waste of good wine at first, but it really gave it a kick. We used to get our wine from this little shop down on 4th street. The fella who ran it, Tony, he had this mustache that curled right up at the ends. Looked just like one of those old-timey cartoon characters. He closed up shop back in '98, I think. Or maybe '99. Shame, really. You just can't find good, personal service like that at the big supermarkets nowadays. You go into a Kroger and nobody even looks you in the eye. 

But, uh... what was I saying? Oh, right, the bank thing. Yeah, when those flashes happen with the voice and the envelope, it definitely feels like I'm reliving the whole awful mess.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms of reliving the robbery and having intrusive memories suggest a diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), which is coded as F43.1 in the ICD-10. The previous candidates were ruled out as the patient's symptoms do not align with personality disorders.

doctor.intent: determine if patient is experiencing avoidance behaviors related to the traumatic event
doctor.question: Have you been avoiding places or activities that remind you of the robbery outside the bank?

target_item.name: Trauma_Avoidance
target_item.manifestation: I've been taking the long way around so I don't pass the bank, and I haven't gone into the festival storage room because it brings the whole thing too close.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking if I have been avoiding places or activities that remind me of the robbery. This corresponds to the 'Trauma_Avoidance' symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, I suppose I have been, yes. I've been taking the long way around when I go for my morning walk, just so I don't have to pass by that bank. It adds about four blocks to my route, which isn't terrible, I guess. Gets the blood pumping. My doctor—Dr. Aris, not the dentist, the general practitioner—he's always telling me I need to keep moving. Says at my age, the joints rust up if you don't use them. He's a young fella, probably not even forty yet. Wears these bright, colorful socks with his fancy suits. Last time I was in, he had flamingos on his ankles. Flamingos! Can you believe it? In my day, a professional man wore black or navy socks. Period. Maybe brown if he was wearing a tweed suit, but that was pushing it. My father was a tailor, you know. Worked down in the garment district for forty-five years. He could spot a cheap suit from across the street. He always said, "A man is only as good as the cut of his trousers." 

But, uh, where was I? Oh, the bank. Yes, I avoid walking past it. And I haven't gone into the festival storage room at the community center, either. I usually help organize the fall festival—been doing it for twelve years now—but I just can't bring myself to go in that room. It just brings the whole thing too close, you know? Makes me feel all tight in the chest.

doctor.intent: determine presence of nightmares related to the robbery
doctor.question: Have you been having any nightmares about the robbery?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about nightmares, which is a symptom of sleep disturbance but specifically refers to distressing dreams. The patient's Sleep_Disturbance symptom (S027) mentions trouble falling asleep and waking up early, but does not mention nightmares. Therefore, there is no exact match in the symptom profile for nightmares.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. I don't think I've had any bad dreams about it. Honestly, I don't remember my dreams much anymore anyway. Usually I just sleep right through the night, unless I have to get up to use the washroom. Which happens more often than I'd like to admit these days. My prostate isn't what it used to be. Dr. Aris gave me some pills for it, little orange things. They taste awful if you don't swallow them fast enough. Reminds me of this orange soda we used to get when I was a kid. Nehi, it was called. Oh, that stuff was sweet. We'd save up our pennies all week just to get a bottle on a hot summer afternoon. We'd sit on the porch steps—my childhood home had these big, wide wooden steps, painted a dark forest green. My mother repainted them every spring without fail. She was a stickler for keeping the house looking sharp. She'd be out there with her brush, wearing this big straw hat with a yellow ribbon. 

But anyway, no, I haven't been waking up in a sweat or anything like that. Just regular sleep, mostly.

doctor.question: Do you find yourself being more aware of your surroundings than usual, like you're constantly on the lookout for something?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hypervigilance (being more aware of surroundings, constantly on the lookout). The patient's symptom profile includes 'Exaggerated_Startle_Response' (jumping at minor stimuli), but does not specifically list hypervigilance.

patient.answer:
Not really, no. I wouldn't say I'm constantly on the lookout or anything like that. I mean, I've always been a bit observant, just by nature. I like to sit by the front window in the afternoons with my tea and just watch the neighborhood go by. You see all sorts of things if you just sit still. Like Mrs. Gable from across the street. She's always out there fussing with her petunias. I swear, that woman waters them three times a day. It's a wonder the poor things haven't drowned yet. Her husband, Frank, he used to have the most beautiful lawn on the block before he passed. Cut it on a diagonal, just like a baseball outfield. He worked at the Chevy plant for thirty-something years before his back gave out. Good union man, Frank was. We used to go bowling down at the alley on 5th Street every Thursday night. Had a team called the Pin Pounders. We even got matching shirts one year, bright blue with our names stitched over the pocket in white thread. Mine shrank in the wash, though, my wife accidentally put it on hot... 

But, uh... I'm sorry, what was the question? Oh, being on the lookout. Right. No, I'm not really looking over my shoulder or feeling jumpy. Just keeping an eye on the street the same as I always have.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of exaggerated startle response
doctor.question: Do you find yourself jumping or startled more easily than you used to, even by small surprises?

target_item.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
target_item.manifestation: When a car backfired near the senior center, I jumped so hard my chest hurt and my hands kept shaking for a few minutes after.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I find myself jumping or startled more easily than I used to, which directly corresponds to the Exaggerated Startle Response symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, I suppose I have been. Just the other day I was walking near the senior center. I go there for the Tuesday morning card games. Pinochle, usually, though sometimes they rope me into bridge. I'm not much for bridge, too much counting, but Arthur insists. Arthur used to be an accountant for the city, so he loves all that math stuff. He's got this little mustache he actually waxes at the ends, looks like something out of an old black-and-white movie. He buys the wax special from some catalog. 

Anyway, I was outside the center, and this car drove past and backfired. Goodness, I jumped so hard my chest actually hurt. My hands just kept shaking for a few minutes after, too. I couldn't even get my keys out of my pocket to unlock my own front door when I got home. You just don't hear cars backfire like that anymore, you know? With all the computers they put in engines these days, they run so quiet. My first car was a '54 Chevy, and that thing rattled so loud you couldn't hear yourself think. The muffler fell right off on Main Street once, just clattered right down onto the pavement in front of the diner. The waitress, Betty, she came out laughing... 

But, what were we talking about? Oh, right, being startled. Yes, that car backfiring really gave me a terrible fright. Shook me right up.

doctor.intent: Determine the duration of the patient's symptoms
doctor.question: How long have you been feeling this way since the robbery outside the bank?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about a week, ever since the robbery outside the bank.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the patient has been feeling this way since the robbery, which directly corresponds to the duration of the symptoms.

patient.answer:
Well, it's been about a week now. Just a week since that awful business outside the bank. I usually go to that branch on Elm Street every Friday morning to get cash for the weekend. I like to have crisp bills, you know? The tellers there are always so nice about it. Especially Sarah, she's a lovely girl. She always asks about my grandson, Tommy. He's at college now, studying engineering of all things. I don't know where he gets the brains for it. His father, my son, he can barely fix a leaky faucet without calling a plumber. I remember when he tried to fix the sink in the downstairs bathroom... oh, it must have been 1985 or so. He ended up flooding the whole hallway. The carpet squished when you walked on it for a week. We had to rent one of those big wet-vacs from the hardware store. Old Mr. Henderson ran the place back then, always had a cigar stub hanging out of the corner of his mouth. He never actually lit it, just chewed on it... 

But yes, to answer your question, it's been about a week since the robbery. Just a week.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of avoidance behaviors related to the robbery
doctor.question: Are there any other activities or places you've been avoiding since the robbery happened outside the bank?

target_item.name: Trauma_Avoidance
target_item.manifestation: I've been taking the long way around so I don't pass the bank, and I haven't gone into the festival storage room because it brings the whole thing too close.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoiding activities or places since the robbery, which directly corresponds to the Trauma_Avoidance symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, I suppose I have been changing my routine a bit. I've been taking the long way around town just so I don't have to pass by that bank. It means I have to walk all the way down Maple Street now, which isn't so bad, really. The oak trees there are just lovely this time of year. My wife and I planted an oak when we first bought our house back in '72. Bought it as a little sapling from a nursery out in the county. The fellow who sold it to us, Jim, he had a glass eye. Always made me wonder how he lost the real one, but you know, it seemed rude to ask. He wore these thick wool sweaters even in the dead of summer. Said it kept the mosquitoes off, but I think he just liked the pockets. 

But... oh, what was I saying? Right, avoiding places. Yes, so I don't go near the bank. And I haven't gone into the festival storage room at the community hall, either. It just... it brings the whole thing too close, you know? I usually help sort the decorations for the autumn jubilee this time of year. We have these big orange and yellow banners we hang right across Main Street. Last year, the wind caught one and it got tangled right up in the traffic light. Took the fire department an hour to get it down with their ladder truck. Chief Miller was hollering at the young volunteers the whole time. He's got a voice like a foghorn, that man... 

But anyway, yes. I just can't bring myself to go in that storage room right now. Or go anywhere near the bank.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life due to the symptoms

target_item.name: Functional Impairment

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulties in daily life or relationships, which directly corresponds to the functional impairment symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, I suppose it has been making things difficult. I haven't been able to keep up with organizing the Día de los Muertos event the way I usually do. I'm usually the one who coordinates the marigold orders, you know. We get them from a wholesale place a few towns over. The fellow who runs it, Carlos, he's been doing it for thirty years. He used to drive this beat-up old green pickup truck, the kind with the wooden side panels. I always told him he should get it painted, but he said the rust gave it character. He's got a dog, too, a big golden retriever mix named Buster who just sleeps right in the middle of the greenhouse aisles. You have to step right over him, and he doesn't even open an eye... 

But, oh, right, the event. Yes, I just haven't been able to focus on it. And I've stopped going to my card nights, too. I just... I don't feel steady around people right now. I used to go every Thursday. We'd play rummy, mostly. Sometimes poker if Frank was feeling lucky. Frank always wears these loud Hawaiian shirts, even in December. He says it keeps his spirits up. He buys them from a catalog that sells nothing but tropical clothing and, for some reason, novelty bird feeders. He got one shaped like a pirate ship once, but the squirrels figured out how to get into the rigging and ate all the suet in one afternoon... 

Anyway, yes. No card nights, and I'm falling behind on the festival planning. It's just too much right now.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant guilt or shame related to the robbery
doctor.question: Have you been feeling guilty or ashamed about anything related to the robbery outside the bank?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of guilt or shame related to the robbery, which corresponds to negative alterations in cognitions and mood (e.g., distorted blame or negative emotional state), but this symptom is not present in my profile.

patient.answer:
Guilty? No, no, I don't think so. I mean, I didn't do anything wrong, did I? I was just standing there. Though, speaking of feeling guilty, my neighbor Mrs. Gable felt terribly guilty just the other day. She backed her car right over my prized petunias. Flattened the whole flowerbed by the mailbox. She drives this enormous beige Lincoln Town Car, you know the kind? They look like boats sailing down the street. My uncle Arthur used to drive a boat of a car like that, a '76 Cadillac Fleetwood. Oh, he loved that thing. Washed it every single Sunday morning with a special chamois cloth he ordered out of a catalog. He wouldn't let anyone else touch the paint, not even his own kids. His youngest boy, Bobby, once drew a little smiley face in the dust on the trunk, and Arthur chased him around the yard with the garden hose for a good ten minutes. Bobby ended up joining the Navy, actually, stationed out in San Diego. I always wondered if that hose incident had something to do with him liking the water... 

But, oh, what were you asking? About the robbery. Right. No, no guilt or shame or anything like that. Just... just trying to get by.

patient.answer:
Well, let me think... no, I don't think there's anything else I've stopped doing. I still go down to the bakery every morning for my coffee, even though it's a bit of a walk now with my new route. The girl who works the counter there, Sarah, she always saves me a blueberry muffin. She's a sweetheart, really. Just got engaged to a boy who works over at the hardware store. He's a nice enough fellow, but he's got this habit of chewing on toothpicks all day long. I asked him once if he was trying to quit smoking, but he said no, he just likes the taste of the wood. Reminds me of my grandfather, actually. He used to whittle these little wooden figures on the front porch. Bears, mostly, sometimes an owl if the wood had a good knot in it. He gave me one for my tenth birthday, a little bear standing on its hind legs. I kept it on my dresser for years until my mother accidentally knocked it off while dusting and chipped its ear. She tried to glue it back on, but she used that old hide glue that smells like wet dog, and it never quite looked the same...

But, um, what was the question? Oh, routines. Right. No, I think I've mentioned everything. Just avoiding the bank and the storage room, mostly.

doctor.question: Do you find yourself constantly looking over your shoulder or feeling like you're waiting for something bad to happen?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hypervigilance (constantly looking over shoulder, waiting for something bad to happen). While I have Exaggerated Startle Response (S080), hypervigilance is a distinct symptom which is not in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not constantly, I don't think. I'm not waiting for anything bad to happen, really. Though my sister, Margaret, she's always waiting for the other shoe to drop. She reads those horoscopes in the Sunday paper like they're gospel. Last week it told her to beware of sudden financial changes, so she went and took all her money out of the credit union and hid it in a coffee can under the sink. It's a Folgers can, the big red plastic ones they make now. Not like the old tin ones. Remember those? My dad used to keep nails in them in the garage. He had dozens of them lined up on a shelf, all labeled with masking tape and a black marker. He had a very specific system for his nails—galvanized, finishing, roofing—and if you put one back in the wrong can, oh, you'd hear about it for a week. He built a whole shed out back just using scrap wood he found behind the old lumber yard. The yard shut down back in... oh, it must have been '85. They built a strip mall there instead, got one of those frozen yogurt places where you pull the levers yourself. I tried the tart flavor once, but it just tasted like sour milk...

But, right, looking over my shoulder. No, I wouldn't say I do that. I just go about my day, you know?

doctor.intent: determine the presence of dissociative symptoms
doctor.question: Have you felt detached from yourself or the world around you since the robbery happened outside the bank?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of depersonalization or derealization (feeling detached from oneself or the world), which is not listed in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Detached? Hmm. No, I wouldn't say that. I feel like myself, mostly. I mean, the world's still the world, isn't it? Though, speaking of the world, my buddy Frank just bought one of those big globe bars for his living room. You know, the ones that look like an antique map of the earth, and then you open the equator and there's bottles of scotch inside? He got it at an estate sale over in Oak Creek. The house belonged to some retired judge who collected clocks. Hundreds of them, Frank said. Grandfather clocks, cuckoo clocks, little mantel clocks that chimed every fifteen minutes. I'd go crazy with all that ticking. I used to have a wristwatch that ticked so loud I had to leave it in the kitchen drawer at night just to get some sleep. It was a Timex, one of those with the expandable metal bands that always pinches the hair on your arm. My wife bought it for me for our silver anniversary. We went to a nice steakhouse that night, the one downtown that burned down a few years ago. They had the best baked potatoes, the size of a football, loaded with real bacon bits, not that artificial stuff that comes in a jar...

But, uh, what were we talking about? Detached. Right. No, no, I don't feel detached or anything like that. Just regular old me.

doctor.question: Do you find yourself being overly alert or watchful, even when there's no apparent reason to be?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hypervigilance (being overly alert or watchful), which is a symptom of Acute Stress Disorder or PTSD. However, my symptom profile does not contain a specific symptom for hypervigilance. It contains Exaggerated Startle Response (S080), but that is specifically about reacting strongly to minor stimuli, not being constantly watchful.

patient.answer:
Watchful? Well, no, I wouldn't say that. I'm not really on edge or anything. Although, speaking of watchful, my neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she's practically the neighborhood watch all by herself. Sits at her front window all day with a pair of binoculars. Those heavy black ones, you know? They look like they belong on a Navy battleship. My uncle Arthur was in the Navy. Served on a destroyer in the Pacific back in the day. He used to send us postcards from all over—Hawaii, the Philippines. He brought back this beautiful silk robe for my mother once, embroidered with these big gold dragons. She wouldn't wear it, though, said it was too fancy for just making breakfast, so she hung it up in the cedar closet upstairs. That closet always smelled so strong, gave me a headache if I stayed in there too long looking for my winter coat. We had these heavy wool coats back then, not like the thin, shiny puffy things people wear now. You'd put one of those wool ones on and feel like you were carrying a sack of potatoes on your shoulders. And if it got wet in the snow? Forget about it, took three days to dry out over the radiator... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, being overly alert. Right. No, no, I just mind my own business, really. I don't feel the need to be on the lookout.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a markedly diminished interest or participation in activities they once enjoyed
doctor.question: Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy doing?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities (anhedonia/negative alterations in cognitions and mood), which is not listed in the patient's symptom profile. patient.answer:
Lost interest? No, I wouldn't say that. I still like my usual routine. I go down to the senior center on Tuesdays for pinochle, same as always. Though, speaking of pinochle, my friend Gary just bought one of those automatic card shufflers. You know, the plastic ones where you split the deck and press a button and it zips them together? Makes a terrible racket. He got it from one of those mail-order catalogs. He gets dozens of them in the mail, the ones selling gadgets you don't really need, like heated steering wheel covers or flashlights that double as radios. I bought a radio flashlight once, back in '99 when everyone was worried about that Y2K bug. We stocked up on canned beans and bottled water. My wife, God rest her soul, she bought so much Spam we were eating it for three years after nothing happened. Spam sandwiches, Spam and eggs, baked Spam with cloves stuck in it like a little ham. It's actually not half bad if you fry it up crispy in a cast-iron skillet. You gotta season the skillet right, though, with a little oil and heat, otherwise everything just sticks to the bottom and it's a nightmare to clean. Cast iron lasts forever if you treat it right. My mother had a pan that must have weighed ten pounds...

But, uh, what were you asking me? Losing interest. Right. No, no, I still enjoy my cards and everything else. Just keeping busy, you know?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoiding places, people, or activities associated with the robbery, which directly corresponds to the Trauma_Avoidance symptom.

patient.answer:
Avoiding things? Well, I suppose... I mean, I have been taking the long way around when I drive to the grocery store so I don't have to pass that bank. And I haven't gone into the festival storage room at the community center, either. It just brings the whole thing too close, you know? Being in there, with all those boxes. Though, speaking of boxes, my daughter Sarah just sent me this enormous care package in the mail. It was packed to the brim with those little foam peanuts. I hate those things, they get everywhere. You open the box and suddenly it looks like it snowed in your living room. They stick to your clothes, the carpet, the cat... Oh, the neighbor's cat, Barnaby, he got into a box of them once and came out looking like a marshmallow. Barnaby's a Maine Coon, huge thing, must weigh twenty pounds. He likes to sleep on top of my car in the summer, leaves these big dusty paw prints all over the windshield. I used to wash my car every Sunday, out in the driveway with a bucket of soapy water and a big yellow sponge. You don't see people doing that much anymore, do you? Everyone just goes to those automatic washes where the big floppy brushes slap against the windows. I went through one of those once and it ripped the antenna right off my old Buick. That was a great car, a '78 LeSabre, rode like a boat on a calm lake. Had these plush velour seats that were so comfortable you could fall asleep at a red light...

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, avoiding things. Yeah, just the bank and the storage room. I just stay away from those spots.
